reference_id: AASHTO Guide for Design of Pavement Structures
reference_title: AASHTO Guide for Design of Pavement Structures, 1993 Edition

sections.title: Design Variables -- Time Constraints
sections.summary: Defines the analysis period (total time span the design strategy must cover, 15-50 years by highway condition per general guidelines) and the minimum/maximum performance period concepts underlying stage construction decisions.
sections.body: The analysis period is the total time span any design strategy (initial pavement plus any planned rehabilitation) must cover; general guideline ranges are 30-50 years for high-volume urban, 20-50 for high-volume rural, 15-25 for low-volume paved, and 10-20 for low-volume aggregate-surfaced highways. Longer analysis periods are increasingly recommended (vs. the historical 20-year convention) for life-cycle economic comparisons. The minimum performance period is the shortest acceptable service life before a rehabilitation stage; the maximum performance period is the practical ceiling on service life a given design strategy can achieve (often controlled by environmental serviceability loss such as swelling/frost heave rather than traffic).
key_points: Analysis period guidelines: 30-50yr high-volume urban, 20-50 high-volume rural, 15-25 low-volume paved, 10-20 aggregate-surfaced
Minimum performance period: shortest acceptable stage service life
Maximum performance period: practical ceiling on service life (may be environmentally, not traffically, controlled)
Longer analysis periods increasingly recommended for life-cycle cost evaluation
tables: Analysis Period guidelines by highway condition
sections.applicability: Setting the design/analysis time horizon before applying the traffic and structural design equations.

sections.title: Design Variables -- Traffic
sections.summary: All design procedures use cumulative expected 18-kip ESAL traffic over the analysis period (w18-hat), converted to mixed traffic via Appendix D. Design-lane traffic w18 = DD*DL*w18-hat, using directional distribution DD (default 0.5, range 0.3-0.7) and lane distribution DL (100% for 1 lane, down to 50-75% for 4+ lanes per direction).
sections.body: Both highway and low-volume-road design procedures are based on cumulative 18-kip ESAL during the analysis period. The mixed-traffic-to-ESAL conversion procedure and detailed equivalency values are in Appendix D. If the planning-furnished traffic represents the cumulative total (both directions, all lanes), it must be factored to the design lane via w18 = DD x DL x w18-hat, where DD is a directional distribution factor (typically 0.5, ranging 0.3-0.7 depending on which direction carries heavier loaded traffic) and DL is a lane distribution factor depending on the number of lanes available in one direction (100% for 1 lane; 80-100% for 2; 60-80% for 3; 50-75% for 4 or more). A cumulative-ESAL-vs-time graph (Figure 2.1) is needed whenever stage construction is anticipated, to separate cumulative traffic into the periods (stages) encountered.
key_points: All design based on cumulative 18-kip ESAL (w18-hat) over the analysis period
w18 = DD x DL x w18-hat (design-lane traffic)
DD (directional distribution): 0.5 typical, range 0.3-0.7
DL (lane distribution): 100% (1 lane) down to 50-75% (4+ lanes)
Appendix D provides the mixed-traffic-to-ESAL conversion (load equivalency factors)
Figure 2.1 (cumulative ESAL vs time) needed for stage-construction planning

sections.title: Design Variables -- Reliability
sections.summary: Table 2.2 gives suggested reliability ranges by functional classification and urban/rural condition (e.g. Interstate/freeway 80-99.9%, local roads 50-80%), derived from a survey of inherent reliability in current state DOT design practice; higher reliability corresponds to more-used facilities. Overall standard deviation So (0.30-0.40 rigid, 0.40-0.50 flexible) is selected per Part I Section 4.3.
sections.body: Reliability concepts are introduced in Part I Chapter 4 and developed fully in Appendix EE (Volume 2). Table 2.2 presents suggested reliability levels surveyed across many state DOT design procedures by functional classification and urban/rural condition. The reliability design factor FR (a function of ZR from Table 4.1 and the selected So) is applied to the traffic prediction w18 inside the design equation. Because reliability now separately accounts for design uncertainty, other design inputs should use best-estimate (mean) values rather than additional built-in conservatism.
key_points: Table 2.2: Interstate/freeway 85-99.9% urban / 80-99.9% rural; principal arterial 80-99%/75-95%; collector 80-95%/75-95%; local 50-80%/50-80%
Higher reliability levels correspond to more heavily used, harder-to-divert facilities
Reliability factor FR is a function of ZR (Table 4.1) and So (0.30-0.40 rigid, 0.40-0.50 flexible)
Because FR handles design uncertainty, other inputs should use best-estimate (mean) values, not conservative ones
tables: Table 2.2: Suggested Levels of Reliability for Various Functional Classifications
sections.applicability: Selecting the design reliability level and So for the flexible/rigid design equations.

sections.title: Performance Criteria -- Serviceability
sections.summary: Serviceability is the Present Serviceability Index (PSI, 0-5); the guide's core design philosophy relates a specific traffic volume to a minimum desired terminal serviceability pt. po (AASHO Road Test observed) = 4.2 flexible, 4.5 rigid; pt=2.5 or higher for major highways, pt=2.0 for lesser volumes; dPSI = po - pt.
sections.body: Serviceability is measured by the Present Serviceability Index (PSI or p), 0 (impossible road) to 5 (perfect road); the guide's serviceability-performance design concept relates a specific total traffic volume to a minimum acceptable pt at the end of the performance period. Terminal (minimum allowable) serviceability selection reflects the lowest index tolerated before rehabilitation becomes necessary: 2.5 or higher for design of major highways, 2.0 for lesser-volume highways. Public-acceptance survey data associated with the AASHO Road Test gives percent of people rating a pt level 'unacceptable': pt=3.0 -> 12%, pt=2.5 -> 55%, pt=2.0 -> 85%. Observed AASHO Road Test initial serviceability po values were 4.2 (flexible) and 4.5 (rigid); dPSI = po - pt.
key_points: PSI ranges 0 (impossible road) to 5 (perfect road)
po (AASHO Road Test observed): 4.2 flexible, 4.5 rigid
pt (terminal serviceability): 2.5+ major highways, 2.0 lesser-volume
Percent rating unacceptable: pt=3.0 -> 12%, pt=2.5 -> 55%, pt=2.0 -> 85%
dPSI = po - pt (design serviceability loss, the ultimate design-equation input)
tables: Terminal serviceability vs percent rating unacceptable
sections.applicability: Setting po/pt/dPSI, a required input to both the flexible and rigid design equations.

sections.title: Performance Criteria -- Allowable Rutting (Aggregate-Surfaced Roads)
sections.summary: Rutting is treated as a performance criterion only for aggregate-surfaced roads (no suitable AC-surface rutting model was available for this Guide); allowable rut depth 1.0-2.0 in, dependent on average daily traffic.
sections.body: Although rutting is a real distress for asphalt concrete surfaces, no design model suitable for incorporation into this Guide was available at the time of writing; rutting is therefore only a performance criterion for aggregate-surfaced roads, where the model addresses serious deformation of the pavement structure and roadbed support (not simple surface rutting correctable by blading). Allowable rut depth typically ranges 1.0 to 2.0 inches depending on average daily traffic.
key_points: Rutting performance criterion applies ONLY to aggregate-surfaced roads in this Guide
No suitable AC-surface rutting model was available for inclusion
Allowable rut depth: 1.0-2.0 in, dependent on ADT
sections.applicability: Low-volume aggregate-surfaced road design (Part II Chapter 4).

sections.title: Performance Criteria -- Aggregate Loss
sections.summary: For aggregate-surfaced roads, reduces effective pavement thickness over time; two printed empirical models estimate aggregate/gravel loss: a US-study bladings-based model GL=(B/25.4)/(0.0045*LADT+3380.6/R+0.467*G), and a Kenya-study annual model AGL=[T^2/(T^2+50)]*f*(4.2+0.92T+0.889R^2+1.88VC) for low-truck-traffic gravel roads.
sections.body: Aggregate loss due to traffic and erosion thins the pavement structure over time, accelerating deterioration. Two models are provided: (1) a bladings-based US study model (limited data, >50% truck traffic sections) GL(in)=(B/25.4)/(0.0045*LADT+3380.6/R+0.467*G) where B=bladings, LADT=design-lane ADT, R=curve radius (ft), G=grade (%); and (2) a Kenya-study annual model more applicable to low-truck-traffic (car-dominated) roads, AGL=[T^2/(T^2+50)]*f*(4.2+0.92T+0.889R^2+1.88VC), with gravel-type factor f (0.37 lateritic, 0.43 quartzitic, 0.28 volcanic, 0.59 coral). A third Brazil-study model, GL=0.12+0.1223(LT) (LT=thousands of loaded trucks), is also referenced. All have significant drawbacks; local aggregate-loss data should be used where possible.
key_points: GL(in) = (B/25.4)/(0.0045*LADT+3380.6/R+0.467*G) -- US bladings-based model
AGL = [T^2/(T^2+50)]*f*(4.2+0.92T+0.889R^2+1.88VC) -- Kenya study, low-truck-traffic gravel roads
Gravel-type factor f: 0.37 lateritic, 0.43 quartzitic, 0.28 volcanic, 0.59 coral
GL=0.12+0.1223(LT) -- Brazil study (loaded trucks, thousands)
All models have serious drawbacks; local data preferred where available
sections.applicability: Aggregate-surfaced (low-volume) road design, estimating total aggregate loss to size the initial surfacing thickness.

sections.title: Material Properties -- Effective Roadbed Soil Resilient Modulus
sections.summary: Recommends AASHTO T274 laboratory resilient modulus testing across seasonal moisture conditions; the Figure 2.3 chart (uf=1.18e8*MR^-2.32) converts seasonal MR values into a single effective (damage-weighted) design MR for flexible pavements designed via the serviceability criteria. A fully worked 12-month example (Figure 2.4) gives effective MR=5,000 psi.
sections.body: For roadbed materials, laboratory resilient modulus testing (AASHTO T274) on samples representative of each primary moisture season is recommended, or correlations with soil properties (clay content, moisture, PI). Because the design equation uses a single MR while soil support varies seasonally, an 'effective' roadbed MR is computed: each season's MR is converted to a relative damage value uf = 1.18x10^8 x MR^-2.32 (Figure 2.3), the uf values are averaged across all seasonal increments, and the effective MR is the value corresponding to that average uf. Frozen-condition practical values of 20,000-50,000 psi and spring-thaw retained modulus of 20-30% of normal summer/fall values are suggested guidelines when direct testing isn't feasible for those extreme seasons. Design sections with within-season coefficient of variation greater than 0.15 should be subdivided into smaller, more uniform sections. This effective MR applies ONLY to flexible pavements designed via the serviceability criteria, not other MR-based procedures.
key_points: AASHTO T274 laboratory testing recommended, across primary moisture seasons
uf = 1.18e8 * MR^-2.32 (relative damage per seasonal MR, Figure 2.3)
Effective MR = value corresponding to the AVERAGE uf across all seasonal increments
Frozen-condition practical MR: 20,000-50,000 psi; spring-thaw retained modulus: 20-30% of normal
Worked 12-month example (Figure 2.4): monthly MR sum(uf)=3.72, avg uf=0.31 -> effective MR=5,000 psi
Applies only to flexible pavements designed via the serviceability criteria
Sections with within-season CoV > 0.15 should be subdivided

equations.description: Relative damage from a seasonal roadbed MR

figures: Figure 2.3: Chart for Estimating Effective Roadbed Soil Resilient Modulus for Flexible Pavements Designed Using the Serviceability Criteria
Figure 2.4: Chart for Estimating Effective Roadbed Soil Resilient Modulus (worked example)
sections.applicability: Determining the MR input to the flexible design equation (Figure 3.1) from seasonally varying roadbed soil test/correlation data.

sections.title: Material Properties -- Effective Modulus of Subgrade Reaction
sections.summary: An effective (seasonally weighted) k-value for rigid pavement design is developed analogously, incorporating subbase characteristics; its determination is an iterative step within the rigid design procedure itself (Section 3.2.1) rather than a standalone precursor calculation.
sections.body: Like the effective roadbed MR, an effective modulus of subgrade reaction (k-value) is developed for rigid design because k is directly proportional to roadbed MR, using the same seasonal lengths/moduli as input. However, because subbase characteristics also affect the design k-value, its determination is included as an iterative step within the rigid pavement design procedure itself (Part II, Section 3.2.1), not as a standalone precursor calculation.
key_points: Effective k-value is analogous to effective roadbed MR but season-and-subbase dependent
Determination is folded into the iterative rigid design procedure (Section 3.2.1), not standalone
sections.applicability: Cross-reference to the rigid pavement k-value procedure (Section 3.2.1).

sections.title: Material Properties -- Pavement Layer Materials Characterization
sections.summary: Elastic (resilient) modulus is the adopted material-quality basis for this Guide. Low-stiffness materials (soils, unbound granular, stabilized, AC) are tested by AASHTO T274 resilient modulus or ASTM D4123 repeated-load indirect tensile test; high-stiffness materials (PCC, high-cement-content stabilized base) use ASTM C469.
sections.body: Although resilient modulus can apply to any material type, the notation MR in this Guide is reserved for roadbed soil; base/subbase/AC/PCC moduli are denoted EBS, ESB, EAC, EC respectively. Relatively low-stiffness materials should be tested per AASHTO T274 (natural soils, unbound granular layers, and even stabilized layers and AC), noting the need for triaxial confinement in unbound materials. Bound/higher-stiffness materials (stabilized bases, AC) may alternatively use the repeated-load indirect tensile test (ASTM D4123), which is simpler to run. Very stiff/brittle materials (PCC, high-cement-content stabilized bases) are difficult to test via the indirect tensile apparatus and should instead use ASTM C469. Correlations developed by a state DOT or other reputable agency (e.g. the ACI correlation Ec=57,000*(f'c)^0.5 for normal-weight PCC) may also be used. As a guideline for successive unbound layers, the ratio of upper-to-lower resilient modulus should not exceed values that produce tensile stresses in the granular layer.
key_points: Elastic (resilient) modulus is the adopted material-quality basis throughout this Guide
Notation: MR (roadbed soil), EBS (base), ESB (subbase), EAC (asphalt concrete), EC (PCC)
Low-stiffness materials: AASHTO T274 (or ASTM D4123 for bound/stabilized/AC)
High-stiffness materials (PCC, cement-stabilized): ASTM C469
Ec = 57,000*(f'c)^0.5 psi (ACI correlation for normal-weight PCC elastic modulus)
Ratio of successive unbound-layer moduli limited to avoid tensile stress in the granular layer

equations.description: PCC elastic modulus from compressive strength (ACI correlation)

sections.applicability: Selecting the appropriate test method/correlation for characterizing each pavement layer material's modulus.

sections.title: Material Properties -- PCC Modulus of Rupture
sections.summary: Required only for rigid design; the mean 28-day third-point-loading flexural strength (AASHTO T97/ASTM C78) is used, not the (lower) construction-specification value; a correction factor converts a construction specification to an estimated mean.
sections.body: PCC modulus of rupture (flexural strength) is required only for rigid pavement design, using the mean value at 28 days by third-point loading. Because reliability is already separately accounted for, the normal CONSTRUCTION specification value (a lower-tail value, e.g. the 10th or 20th percentile of the strength distribution) should NOT be used directly as design input; instead it should be adjusted to an estimated mean via Sc'(mean) = Sc + z*SDs, where z is a standard normal variate depending on the specification's permissible-below-spec percentage PS (z=0.841 at PS=20%, up to z=2.327 at PS=1%). If an agency's practice uses center-point loading, a correlation to third-point loading should be developed.
key_points: Required only for rigid design; mean 28-day third-point-loading value (AASHTO T97 / ASTM C78)
Do NOT use the construction specification value directly (a lower-tail value)
Sc'(mean) = Sc + z*SDs -- converts spec value to estimated mean

equations.description: Estimated mean PCC modulus of rupture from a construction specification value

sections.applicability: Determining the Sc' input to the rigid pavement design equation (Figure 3.7).

sections.title: Material Properties -- Layer Coefficients
sections.summary: Assigns AASHTO structural layer coefficients (a1, a2, a3) for use in SN=a1D1+a2D2m2+a3D3m3. Asphalt concrete a1 from a chart (Figure 2.5, EAC vs a1). Granular base a2 and subbase a3 have BOTH a nomograph (Figures 2.6/2.7, multi-scale CBR/R-value/Texas-triaxial/modulus alignment charts) AND a printed closed-form regression: a2=0.249*log10(EBS)-0.977, a3=0.227*log10(ESB)-0.839. Cement-treated and bituminous-treated base a2 are chart-only (Figures 2.8/2.9).
sections.body: Although the elastic modulus is the adopted material-quality measure, layer coefficients (ai) are still needed because the SN structural-number approach requires them. Figure 2.5 gives a1 for dense-graded AC surface course vs. EAC at 68F (chart only; caution above EAC=450,000 psi). For granular base, Figure 2.6 is a 5-scale alignment nomograph (a2, CBR, R-value, Texas Triaxial class, elastic modulus) with each scale's origin from different state correlations (Illinois for CBR; California/New Mexico/Wyoming for R-value; Texas for Texas Triaxial; an NCHRP project for modulus); the guide ALSO prints an explicit closed-form alternative, a2=0.249*log10(EBS)-0.977, with a worked check (EBS=30,000 psi -> a2=0.14, CBR~100, R-value~85). Figure 2.7 is the parallel granular-subbase nomograph, with printed regression a3=0.227*log10(ESB)-0.839 (worked check: ESB=15,000 psi -> a3=0.11, CBR~30, R-value~60). For cement-treated bases (Figure 2.8, a2 vs 7-day unconfined compressive strength or elastic modulus) and bituminous-treated bases (Figure 2.9, a2 vs Marshall stability or elastic modulus), only the alignment-nomograph form is printed (no closed-form regression). Table 2.3 gives typical unbound-material k1/k2 for the stress-dependent model MR=k1*theta^k2 by moisture condition, used to estimate EBS/ESB stress-state-dependent values.
key_points: SN = a1*D1 + a2*D2*m2 + a3*D3*m3 -- the layer coefficients ai are the SN 'weights'
a1 (AC surface): Figure 2.5 chart only, EAC (psi) vs a1
a2 (granular base): Figure 2.6 nomograph OR printed regression a2=0.249*log10(EBS)-0.977
a3 (granular subbase): Figure 2.7 nomograph OR printed regression a3=0.227*log10(ESB)-0.839
a2 (cement-treated base): Figure 2.8 chart only, vs 7-day UCS or modulus
a2 (bituminous-treated base): Figure 2.9 chart only, vs Marshall stability or modulus
Table 2.3: typical k1 (3,000-8,000 psi base/subbase), k2 (0.4-0.7) for MR=k1*theta^k2
Base/subbase EBS/ESB at the AASHO Road Test were moisture- and stress-state-dependent (Table values, theta=5-30 psi)

Figure 2.7: Variation in Granular Subbase Layer Coefficient (a3) with Various Subbase Strength Parameters

sections.title: Pavement Structural Characteristics -- Drainage
sections.summary: Quality-of-drainage classes (Excellent 2hr to Very Poor no-drain) modify flexible layer coefficients via drainage coefficients mi (Table 2.4, folded into SN=a1D1+a2D2m2+a3D3m3) or rigid design via a drainage coefficient Cd (Table 2.5, in the strength term of the rigid design equation). AASHO Road Test conditions correspond to mi=Cd=1.0 ('fair' drainage).
sections.body: Drainage level or quality is classified by the time needed to remove free water from the pavement structure: Excellent (2 hours), Good (1 day), Fair (1 week, matching AASHO Road Test conditions), Poor (1 month), Very Poor (water will not drain). For flexible pavements, drainage effects are captured via a drainage coefficient mi that modifies the base/subbase layer coefficients in the SN equation (Table 2.4, varying with quality and percent-of-time-near-saturation); the AC surface course's own drainage effect is not considered. For rigid pavements, drainage effects enter as the drainage coefficient Cd directly in the rigid design equation's strength term (Table 2.5). Individual agencies are encouraged to develop drainage criteria for local aggregates/climate.
key_points: Quality of drainage: Excellent (2hr), Good (1day), Fair (1wk, = AASHO Road Test), Poor (1mo), Very Poor (no drain)
Flexible: drainage modifier mi applied to base/subbase layer coefficients (Table 2.4); AASHO Road Test mi=1.0
Rigid: drainage coefficient Cd used directly in the design equation strength term (Table 2.5); AASHO Road Test Cd=1.0
SN = a1*D1 + a2*D2*m2 + a3*D3*m3 -- the m2/m3 drainage modifiers
tables: Table 2.4: Recommended mi Values for Modifying Structural Layer Coefficients of Untreated Base and Subbase Materials in Flexible Pavements
Table 2.5: Recommended Values of Drainage Coefficient, Cd, for Rigid Pavement Design
sections.applicability: Selecting mi (flexible SN calculation) or Cd (rigid design equation) for a given drainage quality and climate exposure.

sections.title: Pavement Structural Characteristics -- Load Transfer
sections.summary: The load transfer coefficient J (Table 2.6) accounts for a rigid pavement's ability to transfer load across joints/cracks (dowels, aggregate interlock, tied shoulders); AASHO Road Test 'protected corner' (dowelled, no tied shoulder) J=3.2. Higher J values apply for higher traffic/thermal conditions; tied PCC shoulders substantially lower the required J.
sections.body: The J-factor accounts for a rigid pavement's ability to distribute load across discontinuities (joints or cracks) via load transfer devices (dowels), aggregate interlock, and/or tied concrete shoulders. J generally increases with traffic (aggregate interlock effectiveness decreases with load repetitions) and with higher thermal coefficients/temperature variation. If dowels are used, diameter is typically the slab thickness/8 (e.g. 1-1/4 in dowel for a 10-in slab), with 12-in spacing and 18-in length as general guidance. Recommended J ranges (Table 2.6): plain jointed/JRCP with asphalt shoulder and load transfer devices, J=3.2 (Road Test 'protected corner'); without devices, J=3.8-4.4; with tied PCC shoulder and devices, J=2.5-3.1; without devices, J=3.6-4.2. CRCP without tied shoulders: J=2.9-3.2 (asphalt shoulder, aggregate interlock only, historically often taken as 3.2); CRCP with tied shoulders: J=2.3-2.9 (recommended 2.6), substantially lower due to the added load-distribution capability of tied shoulders (traffic assumed not to run on the shoulder).
key_points: J accounts for load transfer via dowels, aggregate interlock, and/or tied PCC shoulders
Higher J needed for higher traffic (interlock degrades with repetitions) and larger thermal variation
Dowel sizing guideline: diameter = slab thickness/8; 12-in spacing, 18-in length
JCP/JRCP: J=3.2 (dowelled, no tied shoulder, AASHO Road Test); 3.8-4.4 (no devices); 2.5-3.1 (dowelled + tied shoulder); 3.6-4.2 (tied shoulder, no devices)
CRCP: J=2.9-3.2 (asphalt shoulder); J=2.3-2.9, recommend 2.6 (tied shoulder)
Concrete shoulder >= 3 ft wide, tied, may be considered a 'tied shoulder'
tables: Table 2.6: Recommended Load Transfer Coefficient for Various Pavement Types and Design Conditions
sections.applicability: Selecting the J input to the rigid pavement design equation (Figure 3.7).

sections.title: Pavement Structural Characteristics -- Loss of Support
sections.summary: The loss-of-support factor LS accounts for potential erosion/voiding beneath a rigid slab's subbase, used to correct the effective k-value downward (Figure 3.6) before use in the rigid design equation.
sections.body: Loss of support (LS) corrects the effective modulus of subgrade reaction for the potential loss of support arising from subbase erosion (e.g. under high-traffic-repetition pumping/erosion of untreated or erosion-susceptible stabilized subbases). The LS factor is applied via Figure 3.6 as the final step (Step 8) of the effective-k-value procedure (Section 3.2.1); higher LS corresponds to a greater expected support loss and a lower design k.
key_points: LS accounts for potential subbase erosion / void formation beneath the slab
Applied as the final correction to the effective k-value (Figure 3.6, Section 3.2.1 Step 8)
Higher LS -> lower corrected design k-value
sections.applicability: Final correction step in developing the rigid design k-value (see Section 3.2.1).

sections.title: Reinforcement Variables
sections.summary: Introduces the reinforcement design variables addressed in Section 3.4: for JRCP, distributed steel percentage (subgrade-drag equation); for CRCP, longitudinal steel percentage controlling crack spacing/width.
sections.body: For jointed reinforced concrete pavements, the amount of distributed steel reinforcement needed to hold together the wider transverse cracks that develop between the (longer) joint spacings is designed via the subgrade-drag equation. For continuously reinforced concrete pavements, the longitudinal steel percentage is the primary design variable, controlling the resulting transverse crack spacing and crack width. Full reinforcement design procedures are given in Section 3.4.
key_points: JRCP: distributed steel percentage via the subgrade-drag equation
CRCP: longitudinal steel percentage controls crack spacing/width
Full procedures cross-referenced to Section 3.4
sections.applicability: Introduces the reinforcement variables developed in Section 3.4 (Rigid Pavement Reinforcement Design).
